en: Regarding the establishment and abandonment, and the separation and combination of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu): The verse says:
They are taught according to what increases [affliction], the basis for the notion of "self," the objects of its activity, and their arising;
they are established as supports, parts, and as concise or extensive; there is no distinction in their faculties or their objects.
Regarding the statement that "the basis of the self is taught according to its increase," this refers to the establishment,
exclusion, and combination of the five aggregates as explained in the Abhidharma treatises.
For what reason are there only five aggregates?
It is to manifest the five kinds of objects pertaining to the self (*ātman*):

namely, the object of the self as body and possessions; the object of the self as experience and enjoyment; the object of the self as speech; the object of the self as the performance of all dharmas, both wholesome and unwholesome; and the object of the self as the essential nature that serves as their basis.
The five aggregates are assigned and explained according to their respective order;

therefore, there is neither decrease nor increase, neither separation nor combination. Based on this, the brief and extensive [explanations] concerning the basis, the activity, the arising, and the maintenance are established.
This refers to the establishment of the bases (*āyatana*) through the combination and exclusion of elements (*dhātu*).
Since the meaning of "basis" is the sense of "origination," it is briefly explained as follows:
the support (*āśraya*) and that which is acted upon by it constitute the twelve bases.
Because it is that from which the substance of the six consciousnesses arises, it does not depart from being their locus (*āyatana*).

Since the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the sense of maintaining its own nature (*svabhāva*) and the sense of being able to support [others], it is the basis for the expansion of consciousness and the expansion of this consciousness itself.
Expanding upon these activities,
they constitute the eighteen elements (*dhātus*):
the six faculties, the six objects, which can sustain the six consciousnesses.
The intrinsic nature of the six consciousnesses is able to sustain the function of consciousness;
this nature can maintain itself independently of the [separate] establishment of the elements (dhātu).
This nature does not arise of itself.

Since they are not established as bases (āyatana) apart from the six consciousnesses, the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) neither decrease nor increase; they involve separation and conjunction, yet there is no separate faculty or object.

Explanation of the Seventh and Eighth: The reason why the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are not separately established as bases (*āyatana*) or elements (*dhātu*) is that, apart from the faculties and objects of the six consciousnesses, there are no other distinct faculties or objects that could be established as elements or bases; therefore, they are not so established.
The second chapter of the *Madhyāntavibhāga* explains the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The verse says:
"Not one, and being a collective summary."
The meaning of "segmentation" is *skandha* (aggregate);
the meanings of "grasper," "the grasped," and "the seeds of that grasping" are *dhātu* (element).
The sense bases (*āyatana*) are so named in the sense of being the "gateways" through which the perceiving faculty experiences the objects it cognizes;
this is explained in detail as stated therein.
The ten types of threefold categories are as explained in the *Abhidharma-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
Herein, they should be analyzed by way of three gates:
first, the explanation of their names and meanings.
Second, the establishment and abandonment [of categories].
There are thirty kinds of distinctions;
such are these various characteristics.
In the section on the inquiry into arising, the distinct views of the three masters—Śubhagupta and the others—are presented.
Their respective characteristics are all provisionally designated based upon the transformations of consciousness;
it is regarding these that worldly people give rise to grasping.
The holy teachings explain this based on this meaning;
the grasped [nature] and the dependent [nature] are explained separately as appropriate.
This is the interpretation of Dharmapāla and Nanda; the interpretation of Sthiramati states:
The two kinds [of consciousness] are based on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Furthermore, they are explained in the same way as below.
Those images (*nimitta*) depend solely on the seeing and image portions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*), which are termed "that which is transformed.
As for the distinct explanation from what follows:
In this context, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is also that which is transformed.

The following point—that it universally depends upon both the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—is accepted by both ancient and modern scholars alike, and is established by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
It depends solely upon the aspect of the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
This is based on actual dependence; thus, both are self-attesting,
because seeds transform to manifest as active states,
and active states likewise transform to become seeds.
Because *tathatā* (suchness) is not a support (*āśraya*), it is not mentioned in the treatise.
Regarding the view that the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) arise from the same seed (*ekabīja*) or different seeds (*nānābīja*),
there are two interpretations.
Some say that the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) arise from the same seed,
meaning that when there is no underlying substance (*svabhāva*),
the image-aspect and the seeing-part arise from the same seed.
Regarding those that possess a substantial essence (svabhāva),
their essence likewise arises from seeds; that is,
when a single seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) arises as a manifest state (pravṛtti) from its seed.
Because the three phenomena belong to the same kind—
namely, the reflection, the image, and the object.
Some say that the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and the reflection arise from different kinds.
The essential nature and the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) necessarily arise from distinct seeds;
as for their image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga),
it is [identical] with the seeing-part and the essential nature.
They may be either different or the same.
Because the seeds and the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the manifesting consciousnesses act as causes and conditions for one another, they are both primordially existent and co-emergent.
Alternatively, the manifesting objective parts may arise through synthesis, because the new and old seeds arise together. Anavai also states that both parts [of consciousness] arise from seeds.
The seeing [faculty] is identical to its substance.
Regarding the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga), there are two theories:
that it is either identical or different [from the substance].

The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) lacks substantial reality, and the seeds are provisional. According to the correct principle of Dharmapāla, there are three factors: the two aspects—the substance and the reflection—and the seeing-aspect (darśana-bhāga).
These three do not necessarily all share the same nature, seeds, realm-attachment (dhātu-bandhana), and so forth.

Because it corresponds to what is appropriate, the previously stated position that the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) have distinct seeds is the correct meaning. The verse says:
The objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) does not follow the mind; The solitary image (*pratibimba-mātra*) follows only the seeing-aspect.
The "mixed" (sābhāsā) [object] involves both the mental state (*caitta*) and the fundamental nature (*svabhāva*).
There are three categories that collectively encompass all objects according to their respective natures: first, the "objective reality" (*tattvaviṣaya*).
The actual entities of all phenomena are termed objective realities.
Form is true form;
mind is the real mind.
This dharma of reality is not fixed, nor does it follow the three natures of the mind.
The five objects as they truly are are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because they do not conform to the three natures of the five consciousnesses that take them as objects,
nor do they conform to the mind by sharing its same level of bondage (*bandhana*).
Just as the eighth consciousness belongs to a single realm-connection (dhātu-bandhana),
its objects— the seeds— pervade all three realms;
when one is in a lower realm and gives rise to the two supernormal powers, it takes the divine eye and divine ear as its objects.
When the body is in a higher stage, the eye and ear consciousnesses perceive objects of the desire realm;
from the second dhyāna upward, the eye, ear, and body consciousnesses take objects belonging to their own stage.
Consciousness is bound to the first dhyāna,
while its object is bound to its own level;
such categories likewise do not arise from a single type of mind.

Because the nature, category, and seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are each distinct; whereas for the second type, the object consisting solely of a mental projection (*pratibimba*), its nature, category, and seeds are all necessarily identical to those of the seeing-part alone.
Just as the sixth consciousness takes as its objects such things as tortoise hair, flowers in the sky, or a barren woman’s son,
as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and objects belonging to other realms—
such categories are all merely in accordance with the mind.
It has no separate essence or function, as it is subsumed under the category of provisional objects;
therefore, it is called "solely projected" (duoying). Third is the object that carries a substantial reality (dai zhi zhi jing).
This means that this image possesses a real primary substance (*mūlabhāva*),
such as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) transformed by the seventh consciousness within the causal state; thus,
it can be categorized as non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) based on its primary substance.
It is also subsumed under the "obscured" category by virtue of its seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
It may be said to arise from seeds of the objective essence (*nimitta-bhāga*),
and it may also be said to arise from seeds of the seeing-part.
Because the meaning is not fixed: regarding "the nature-seed and so forth according to what is appropriate," "according to what is appropriate" is an indeterminate term.
There are two kinds of "according to what is appropriate."
First, the meaning clarifies that when various mental aggregates arise,
there are cases where there is only one [object].
There are two [types] that are combined, and three that are gathered together.
Regarding "there is one," it is as has already been explained previously. Regarding "there are two that are combined":
Just as the eighth consciousness takes dispersed objects of its own stage as its cognitive object,
that which is the cognitive object of the mind-king (citta) is a primary objective realm (*tattva-viṣaya*),
whereas that which is the cognitive object of the mental factors (*caitta*) is a solitary shadow-realm (*pratibimba-viṣaya*).
The objects of the five consciousnesses are the five sensory objects of their own level;
these are the first type of objective realm (xing-jing).
They may also be described as realms that carry a substantial essence (dai-zhi zhi-jing).
Just as the sixth consciousness takes the past and future five aggregates as its object and thus obtains a "solitary image" (duoying),
it may also be said to take an "object with substance" (dai zhi zhi jing).
Because it perfumes [the mind] to produce seeds that give rise to the substantial entity (svabhāva),
there are three types of conjunctions.
For example, as in the case where the fourth dhyāna and the eighth consciousness take the matter produced by meditative concentration (samādhi-phala-rūpa) as their object.
The objects of mental factors (*caitta*) are exclusively "solitary shadows" (*duoying*);
the objects of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) are objects of real nature (*shixingjing*),
which may also be described as "objects bearing substance" (*dazhijing*).

Because the sixth [consciousness] takes as its essential nature the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). Second, regarding the phrase "the nature-seeds (*prakṛti-bīja*) and so forth, as appropriate," this indicates that the three aforementioned objects apply according to their respective suitability.
Alternatively, although their nature may be the same, their fetters (*saṃyojana*) and categories (*prakāra*) may differ—
as in the case of the divine eye and ear belonging to a lower stage that take a higher realm as their object.
Or, although their fetters may be the same, their nature and categories may differ.
Just as the five consciousnesses take the five objects of their own realm as conditions,
or as there may be cases where the seeds are identical yet their bonds differ—
when considered in terms of their aggregation, they exist.
If one analyzes this according to the theory of a single dharma, it is non-existent.
For example, within the collection of mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness, the objects of the [mental factors] and the seeing [part] are of the same kind;
yet, while the objects of the mind-king [the primary consciousness] are the same, their respective attachments (bandhana) differ.
The principles for combining two and three [syllables] may be understood by analogy.
By means of this single verse, the essence of all dharmas—
whether cause or fruit— is definitively established within the eight consciousnesses.
Each individual aspect is set forth separately for each of the five aggregates;
fearing prolixity, I shall stop here.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) means that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two parts.
Having explained that which is transformed by consciousness,
based on these two aspects, the following section explains the transformer and the transformed;
for both the self and dharmas are equally dependent upon what is transformed by consciousness.
If one were to divide the text into two sections based on its general structure,
the first section would explain the third phrase:
"Alternatively, internal consciousness transforms and appears as external objects."
The section beginning with "Because of the power of the habitual tendencies of the discrimination of self and dharmas" explains the transformation of the subject and the object;
the subsequent section explains the subjective and objective supports.
The section "That which is conceived by the foolish is inferior" is divided into two parts.
Regarding "the subject and object of transformation":
Regarding "that which is transformed by consciousness" and "the support of the subject and object":
it refers to that [consciousness] as the basis.
In the passage beginning with "By the power of the habitual perfuming of the discrimination of self and dharmas," there are two difficulties.

The first asks: when the various consciousnesses arise as semblances of self and dharmas, do they all do so solely through the power of the habitual perfuming of the discrimination of self and dharmas?
It is also not due to them.
If it were due to both,
then the eight consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses would be indistinguishable in their lack of dualistic discrimination.
When the subsequent fruit arises, it should not resemble those two.
If it does not [resemble them], why is it stated here that only the perfuming of self and dharmas serves as the cause? Answer: Both interpretations are valid.
All of these arise from conceptualization (*vikalpa*):
because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are accompanied by the two types of conceptualization within the seventh consciousness,
or because they are induced by the two types of conceptualization of the sixth consciousness.
When they subsequently produce their fruits, these all resemble my own dharmas;
it is not necessarily through understanding [them].
This explains the sixth fundamental [consciousness], which universally conditions everything.
Because they act as causes and conditions that give rise to the various consciousnesses and cause them to be perfumed,
when the subsequent fruits arise, they manifest in the likeness of the marks of a self and phenomena; or,
though not external, they appear as if external.
Because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are reckoned as arising in a manner similar to external objects,
if Master An-hui held that all eight consciousnesses possess grasping (*sgrub pa*),
this question would not be necessary.
Regarding the term "like one in a dream":
*vāraṇa* means "transmigration" (*liúzhuǎn*) in this language;
it is a corruption of the earlier term *pravrajan*.
This King Saṃsāra was the king of the kingdom of Mūḍhava;
he was handsome in appearance and considered himself peerless.
Seeking a superior form with which to compare himself and manifest his own excellence,
he heard someone say:
"In the city of Rājagṛha, there is Mahākātyāyana."
Her appearance was exceedingly beautiful,
peerless in the world;
the King sent messengers to welcome her.
Kātyāyana arrived.
The king went out from the palace to meet him;
the king could not catch up with him.
The people looked upon Kātyāyana as they did not look upon the king.
When the king asked for the reason,
the assembly informed him.
Kātyāyana’s appearance surpassed that of the king.
The king asked the Venerable One about the causes from his past lives that resulted in this present fruit.
Kātyāyana replied:
In the past, when I had gone forth into the homeless life,
the king was a beggar;
I swept the floors of the monastery.
When the King came to beg for alms,
I first had him sweep the ground and then ordered him to remove the refuse;
only after the removal of the refuse was completed did I give the King food.
By virtue of these karmic causes, he was reborn among humans and devas, obtaining the retribution of an upright and handsome appearance.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately requested to leave the household life and become a disciple of Kātyāyana.
Later, he went together with Kātyāyana to the country of Avanti.
While he was practicing the Way in the mountains and sitting in meditation in a secluded place,
King Abhaya, whose name was Bimbisāra,
led his court ladies into the mountains for recreation.
The palace attendants, seeing that King Bimbisāra’s appearance was handsome and upright,
gathered around to gaze at him. King Bimbisāra, seeing King Prasenajit,
suspected he had lustful intentions and asked Prasenajit:
"Are you an arhat or not?
The king replied, "No.
Subsequently, he asked each of the others regarding the remaining three fruits of spiritual attainment, and they all replied, "No."
He asked again, "Have you abandoned desire?
He answered again, "No.
Patraśāta said in anger:
If that is so, why did you, among my eight courtesans,
whip your body until it was broken and you fell unconscious in death,
only regaining consciousness at night to come before Kātyāyana?
Upon seeing him, Kātyāyana felt compassion in his heart.
His fellow students asked how he might be treated.
King Pāṭaliputra said to Kātyāyana:
"I beg leave of my teacher to return briefly to my own country to assemble an army,
destroy that kingdom of Abhaya,
and slay King Bhaṃśudāsa."
"When my business is finished, I shall return to follow my teacher and cultivate the Way.
Kātyāyana accepted his request and said to the king,
"I wish to depart, but please allow me to stay for one night."
Kātyāyana placed him in a favorable position and put him to sleep,
intending for him to have a dream; in the dream,
he saw himself assembling an army to campaign against Abhanyā.
His own army was defeated and he himself was captured by the enemy.
His hands and feet were bound tightly, a red flower was stuck in his hair, and the execution drums were beaten as he was about to be put to death.
In his dreams, the king cried out in terror with a broken voice, saying:
"I now have no refuge.
I pray that you, Master, will deliver me and act as my place of refuge so that I may attain a long life.
Kātyāyana, by means of his supernatural power, produced fire from his finger and called out to him to awaken.
He asked, "For what reason?
His mind was not yet clear, and he still spoke of the calamity.
Kātyāyana shone a light upon him with fire and questioned him.
"What place is this?
You should look for yourself.
Only then did his mind awaken.
Kātyāyana said, "If you attack him,
he will surely be defeated and ruined, just as one sees in a dream.
The king said, "I pray that you, Master, will rid me of this poisonous intent."
Kātyāyana explained to him that all phenomena are like a country,
which is a mere conventional designation without reality;
apart from houses and such, there is no separate country.
Thus it is explained at length through various causes and conditions,
up to the point that even a single atom is not a substantial reality;
there is neither "this" nor "that," neither enmity nor affection.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the king attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Subsequently, he gradually attained the fruit of an arhat.
Regarding the statement that "objects exist only conventionally" (saṃvṛti-sat):
The Commentary offers two interpretations.
Now, furthermore, it is added:
because they are objects of the universal imagination (parikalpita) of ordinary beings, they exist only conventionally (saṃvṛti).
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the object of the wisdom of both ordinary beings and noble ones; consciousness is also the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
This is shown by including both [aspects].
Within the refutation of the self (*ātman*), [this is demonstrated].
The Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools establish their own tenets, asserting:
"The self and the nature of the self are eternal,
for they are admitted to be without beginning or end."
Furthermore, the essence of the self is all-pervading,
because it is admitted to be eternal,
like space and so forth. Like space and so forth.
The thesis previously established serves as this reason:
the self-entity is eternal and omnipresent,
for it is admitted that it undergoes pleasure, pain, and so forth, in accordance with the body through which karma is performed.
Regarding the initial measurement of the great void,
there is the fault of contradicting the specific characteristics of the existent dharma (dharmin).
This refers to the meaning intended by me upon the existent dharma.
"I experience suffering through karma created in accordance with the body;
I experience pleasure through karma not created in accordance with the body"—
this is the distinction between the self that possesses phenomena (*sadharmaka-ātman*) and the self itself.
Now, a contradiction is raised:
"According to you, I should not experience suffering or pleasure in accordance with the body,
because you assert that the self has neither beginning nor end."
Like great empty space, it is difficult for a second measure [to apply].
There is the fault of contradiction with the specific characteristics of the modes of operation;
for the intended meaning is that the essence is eternal, pervasive, and a self-characteristic of phenomena.
The suffering resulting from karma created in accordance with the body is not the same as the bliss whose essence is eternal and pervasive;
this is the distinction between the two.
Now, a contradiction is asserted:
"According to you, I should not experience suffering or pleasure resulting from karma created in accordance with the body,
because [the self] is admitted to be permanent."
Regarding the third member of the syllogism, it is stated:
Since the reason that conforms to the body is unestablished for at least one [of the two parties] and is absent from the similar example, space, [the argument fails].
This is precisely the uncommon indeterminate [reason].
In the thesis that [space] is eternal and omnipresent, space serves as the similar example (*sapakṣa*) and the jar serves as the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*).

Regarding the two [positions] that the causes such as karma created while accompanying the body are both non-existent, the treatise raises a counter-objection based on a distinct inference (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), stating: "According to your view, the self should not experience the fruits of karma created while accompanying the body."
Because it is admitted to be permanent and omnipresent,
like great empty space;
this specific point is established by means of inference (anumāna).
One need not state its original measure. The Proponent of Disconnection (Vaimukhya) establishes the following syllogism:
The self described [by the opponent] is not fixed with respect to the body.
Because it belongs to the body,
it is like a shadow and so forth.
In the subsequent objection, one should say:
I should be subject to disintegration,
because it is grasped as being co-extensive with the body,
just like a shadow and so forth.
There is no need to explain the meaning of "following the body" (*anugata*) by means of "retracting and extending.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 6 and 64, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 10,
state that there are four ways of clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*).
First, it is identical to the aggregates (*skandha*).
Second, it is distinct from the aggregates yet abides within them.
Third, it is distinct from the aggregates and abides within dharmas apart from the aggregates.
The four [marks] are distinct from the aggregates; they do not abide within the aggregates,
nor do they abide within dharmas distinct from the aggregates,
yet there are no aggregates.
All phenomena of the aggregates are entirely inconsistent [with this].
The latter three are all included within the conceptualizations of distinct aggregates;
together, these two categories of conceptualization exhaustively encompass the first two types.
He refutes only the non-Buddhists and does not refute the Śrāvakayāna;

therefore, there is no [contradiction] with the teaching that [the self] is neither identical to nor distinct from the aggregates. Furthermore, regarding the refutation of [the self as being] neither identical to nor distinct [from the aggregates], there is this formal inference (*pramāṇa*):
The self that you maintain should not be described as "this is my self" or "this is not another's self," because you admit that it is inexpressible.
Although the point regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned might be so, it does not accord with the meaning of the text;
for it would merely refute a single self rather than all selves.
Furthermore, this treatise merely refutes the self-assertion of a single teacher,
rather than all [teachers];
this interpretation, however, universally refutes them all.
Furthermore, it would suffice to cite a single phenomenon as a concordant example;
why rely on both existence and non-existence?
Moreover, the treatise generally intends for the aggregates of self and non-self to likewise be inexpressible.
Just as there are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how can it be said that "the conditioned is mine" or "the unconditioned is not another's self"? Therefore,
one should follow the commentary.
Within the function of destruction, there are briefly four categories:
first, it has utility with respect to saṃsāra,
but no utility with respect to nirvāṇa.
Second, the Sāṃkhya and others lack the activity of movement and transformation,
whereas others possess this function.
Third, the Vaiśeṣika lacks the functions of acting and experiencing.
The four correct refutations are purposeful;
a refutation that is useless [is not accepted]. Although the Abhidharma texts state that "desire and greed are called grasping," [this does not contradict our position].
The same [text] also explains the member of grasping (*upādāna*) in the tenth stage, stating: "Grasping is defined as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) being predominant.
This is an increase according to the meaning [of the term], not the actual principle.
To speak according to reality:
The *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are called the "appropriation" (*upādāna*) member;
the same applies to the aggregates (*skandha*).
The aggregates are capable of producing appropriation.
Like a fruit-bearing tree,
the aggregates arise from grasping like a fire of grass and chaff;
the eighth consciousness is the objective referent for the seven consciousnesses.
Because it is spontaneously directed toward that which is of the same bond as the view,
six [factors] are spontaneously directed.
One should consider why they are bound collectively or individually, and whether they belong to the same or different levels (bhūmi).
This binding occurs according to the manifestation of the object of perception (ālambana), not according to its seeds (bīja).
The "moistening birth" refers to the conditions for future birth.
The eighty-eight [afflictions] take the dharmas of the three realms as their objects.
The followers of the Two Vehicles first subdue them through cultivation and then enter the Path of Seeing.
Some say that the two types of afflictions— those abandoned through cultivation and those abandoned through seeing— are severed simultaneously and instantaneously,
because the momentum [of the afflictions] has already been broken by the prior aspiration and seeking of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).
Others say they are severed by separately arising paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Now, we adopt the view of simultaneous severance rather than sequential severance.
Regarding the phrase "arising from the marks of one's own mind," there are two interpretations.
One says it refers to the marks of the reflected image.
The second [type] refers to the characteristics as they are grasped.
Although they lack substantial reality, they appear in accordance with the mind's perception;
one should know that all explanations regarding the characteristics of the mind follow this same principle.
Regarding the statement that "these two forms of self-grasping are subtle and thus difficult to sever," the *Sū* (the Commentary) provides three interpretations.
The first takes the aspect of the views and mental formations of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
They are subtle because they are perceived during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
or, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are subtle in relation to the preceding eight stages.
Second, they are called subtle because they are easily abandoned by means of the path of seeing.
The upper paths are difficult to eliminate and are thus termed "coarse," just as within the three minds there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle; likewise,
the three [lower] paths of seeing are [considered coarse] because their counteractive paths are weak.
The characteristics of what is to be abandoned are called "subtle" with respect to the first category;
regarding the path of cultivation, they are called "subtle" in terms of their own category’s mode of activity. There are also three [reasons] why they are difficult to sever:
first, they are not subdued by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Second, the initial path of gradual cultivation is not abandoned,
because it is not something to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Third, the deficient path is not eliminated.
Because it is only when the path of the nine grades is fully perfected that one can effect abandonment.
Now, regarding the fourth [point], if a person who has transcended to the third fruit is grasped by the sixth consciousness,
there are five explanations therein.
The path of seeing cannot sever it;
even after transcending to the attainment of the fruit, it is still not severed.
It must wait until the vajra-like mind, at which point it is severed simultaneously with the grasping of the seventh consciousness.
Second, it is said that one transcends to the stage of fruition by means of a distinct path of abandonment.
Since that [distinct path] does not obstruct the fruition itself,
why is it called the "affliction of that stage"?
What contradiction is there in the seventh consciousness likewise grasping this?
Regarding the three types of transcendence and the attainment of the fruit:
after the path of insight (darśana-mārga), one does not again emerge from meditative absorption to separately initiate superior paths, such as the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and so forth.
One attains the third fruit by abandoning the afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In all other instances, the attainment of the fruit is established as being comprised within the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) at the sixteenth moment of mind;
why, then, is it said here that one attains the fruit by subsequently arising on the path of cultivation to abandon the afflictions?
Because that [tradition] states that the first fruit is not attained through leaping;
when one attains the fruits by leaping through four stages,
one enters the path of cultivation immediately from the path of vision.
In the case of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one abandons the afflictions through cultivation and attains the fruit;
this occurs without the arousal of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because there is no possibility of separately arousing a path of preparation.
This is the fifth instance of attaining the fruit by means of leaping over.
Thus, in a single moment of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the afflictions of both the uninterrupted path and the path of cultivation are simultaneously severed.

According to the first interpretation,

even the preceding eight paths do not eliminate them,

Because its force is firm and stable.

The view that the self is annihilated prior to the aggregates is abandoned because it is coarse and violent; thus,
the fourth [view] is explained as indeterminate.
In each of the nine stages, there are both coarse and subtle [afflictions].
The coarse ones are eliminated first;

Because the active states (caryā) are sometimes coarse and sometimes subtle,
their abandonment occurs sequentially;
such is the case for the various afflictions and their outflows (niṣyanda).

Regarding the statement that "the sequential abandonment is explained according to their categories" and that "recollection and cognition are possible due to the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*)," it is asked:

it is not necessary for this cause to produce this very same fruit.

Because it is admitted that the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) grasp [their objects], they are established as having resistance.
Within the refutation of the category of "that which possesses," there are four parts.
The first fault is that it contradicts the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon itself. He says:
"There is existence."
Apart from the real categories (padārtha), there exists a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because it is admitted not to be non-existent,
just like qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).
This [reason] is indeterminate,
because the "real entity" (vastu) serves as a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta),
since the reason exists therein.
Now it is said:
apart from the phrase "reality," there is no separate intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
for it is admitted that it is not non-existent.
Just as with the "real phrase" (yathābhūtapada),
if those non-Buddhist teachers were to argue that because qualities and actions are distinct from their causes, their conjunction constitutes the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
This is not an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*),
because the opponent's [reason] is inconclusive and it is not common to both [the proponent and the opponent].
Since the treatise uses virtue and karma as the corroborative example (sapakṣa), it merely contradicts inference (*anumāna-viruddha*).
Furthermore, there is the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the subject (*dharmin*) in the second [reason]. He says:
There is existence.
Apart from the real, there is a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because it is admitted to be different from the real.
Just as with the case of virtue and action,
where existence is taken as the existent phenomenon,
what is now called "existence" should not [itself] be existence.
Therefore, it constitutes a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an existent phenomenon (*bhāva*).
Now, taking a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva*) as an example,
it likewise constitutes a contradiction of certainty (*niścaya-viruddha*).
The third and fourth [reasons] both contradict inference (*anumāna-viruddha*).
Among the objections regarding identity and difference,
the first commits the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the subject (*dharmin*).
He says: "The nature of identity and difference must exist as distinct real entities."
Because you admit that difference is real—
just as in the case of qualities and activities— you now claim that both identity and difference are neither identical nor different. Therefore,
this constitutes a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).
How can it also be called "denying that [substance] is different from [quality and action]"?
This reason not only demonstrates that there is a difference between substance and quality or action,
but also demonstrates that the nature of substance and so forth is not the nature of substance and so forth.
Just as it is able to establish the negation of substantiality,
so too is it able to establish the negation of sameness and difference,
because both are equally certain.

Therefore, it constitutes a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*); furthermore, there are not only contradictions through inference (*anumāna*) and through certainty, but also contradictions with the specific characteristic of the subject.
Thus, the treatise uses the word "also" (*api*).
Otherwise, such statements would be useless. As for the fault of contradicting inference (*anumāna-virodha*):
substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) have no other distinct nature [than these three].
6. Because it is subsumed under any one of the ten categories, such as "existence" (mahāsattā) and so forth;
or else, its nature as a real entity is definitively non-existent.
Because it is admitted that [the self] is real,
just as [the self is real], so too would other qualities and the nature of karma likewise be established;
thus, there is also a definitive contradiction.
The objection that "it is neither real nor unreal" is likewise refuted by this same argument;
since it merely employs the term "reason" (hetu), it is not a valid objection.
The third [point] follows the above by reversing the two challenges;
while there is a distinction between the general and the specific, there is no difference in their underlying meaning or principle. The fourth [point] contradicts inference (*anumāna*). It says:
The nature of reality (dharmatā) has no distinct nature,
because it is accepted as being neither the first nor the third [of the three natures].

Just as in the case of "great existence" (*mahāsattā*) and so forth, not only does it fail to establish a common example due to its absence, resulting in an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*),
but it also constitutes a contradiction with inference (*anumānaviruddha*).
The fifth [reason] likewise constitutes a contradiction with inference.
In the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that refutes the existence of consciousness as a real self-nature,
the category of qualities (*guṇapada*)— namely, mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*)— must be excluded.

The four reasons in this treatise refute the preceding positions in the following order; yet,
they also serve as causes for one another.
It should be understood according to reason that the same objection against the [three] propositions can also be applied to the single cause,
as stated in the *Śabdavidyā* (Treatise on Phonetics).
The fifteenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Regarding the establishment of the designation of the locus and the root:

The root of sound is called the "phoneme" (*akṣara*),
which is the syllable itself.
To distinguish the locus of the sound is termed the "place of articulation."
This refers to the declaration that at the beginning of the eon,
Brahmā created one million verses of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*).
Later, it was entrusted to Maudgalyāyana, who abridged it to one hundred thousand stanzas. Subsequently, Śakra further condensed it to ten thousand stanzas.
After that, there was the seer Kātyāyana.
It was abbreviated to twelve thousand stanzas.
Next, there was the sage Pāṇini, who abbreviated it to eight thousand stanzas.

the former two treatises have both already vanished.
The *Śabdānuśāsana*, which deals with the roots and structure of script forms, consists of three hundred verses.

they are known as the *Saṃkṣiptasāra-kārikā*.
Following these are the Eight Treatises on the [Eight] Categories (*Aṣṭādhyāyī*).
There are eight hundred verses titled *Nidāna*. Furthermore,
there is the *Śākyapraśna-śāstra* which has been heard.
There are one thousand five hundred verses.
Furthermore, there is the Vinaya-uttara-grantha,
consisting of two thousand five hundred verses.
These five branches of grammar are collectively termed "Root-Cuts" (*mūla-vyākaraṇa*),
because they serve as the fundamental basis for generating knowledge and understanding within the primary field of grammar.
However, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla...
He composed twenty-five thousand stanzas entitled the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra Miśra-ratna*.
This is regarded in the West as the ultimate and most definitive treatise on grammar.
It is widely prevalent in the world.
However, the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Grammar) consists of five sections.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Continuity, designation, summary, its benefit, and exposition.
First, continuity:
this first section consists of a single chapter on the synthesis of sounds and syllables.
Second is the names and titles.
It is explained that at the beginning of the kalpa, the Brahmā King established one thousand names for each and every dharma;
later, Śakra reduced them to one hundred names.
Later, it was further reduced to ten names;
later still, it was reduced to three names,
forming a single category in total.
This is the second section, titled "The Chapter on Names and Designations.
It consists of three general summaries;
it is the fundamental compendium within the science of grammar (śabdavidyā).
Fourth is "benefiting others.
This is omitted from the intermediate [summary].
Causing sentient beings to give rise to understanding is what is meant by "benefiting others."
The fivefold exposition is the extensive exposition; that is to say,
the concise, the intermediate, and the extensive.

Among the three schools of phonetics (śabdavāda),
there is one that maintains that all sounds are eternal.
There are two interpretations.

The second [view] says that all [sounds] are partially so;
that is, only internal sounds are entirely eternal.
Although there are these two interpretations, the former interpretation is superior.
Although external objects do not themselves express [meaning],
they nonetheless serve as conditions for the production of sound;
furthermore, there is a commonality among all such objects.
There are also individual [refutations] as appropriate.
There are three parts to the refutation of the Sarvāstivāda.
First, a general refutation of the school's tenets;
second, a specific refutation;
third, a conclusion regarding their falsity.
There are three types of refutation.
The first is the treatise on the observation of the common object;
the second can be understood through inference.
The third inference states:
The composite atom does not possess a distinct substantial characteristic apart from the fundamental atoms.
Because at the time they are not combined, they are atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Just as when they are not combined,
so it is with the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).
Briefly, they are distinguished by way of five categories:
first, the provisional and the real;
second, the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
