The discrimination of maturation and so forth; 3.
The discrimination of the objects of consciousness.
The atom (paramāṇu).
Fivefold analysis. First, the discernment of the visual object-condition (cakṣur-ālambana).
Second, resolving contradictions;
third, explaining the benefits;
fourth, identifying which mental factors perform the contemplation.
These are acquired through application and are not innate.
As for the five types of cognitions that take these as objects, to which truths do they belong?
Those that are with outflows (sāsrava) pertain to both truths.
It is subsumed under the noble truth of the path free from outflows;
however, it is not exclusively suffering,
as it extends to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
One grasps [them] as being substantially existent because one observes them through correct contemplation;
it is not only the Truth of Suffering.
However, as for "distinguished by the limits of good or evil according to intention and vow," this is a specific phrase concerning the unmanifest [form] of the Buddha-body,
while it is a general phrase for other manifest and unmanifest [forms].
Although the Buddha’s unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) was acquired in the past and does not arise anew in every moment, it was established by his former vow:
"I shall continue until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted. Thus, his volition regarding karma remains constrained by that original resolve.
Because the mind is without decline or exhaustion,
it is either always present; or,
with the exception of the Buddhas, it has perhaps never been attained by others.
Because one restrains the mind through aspiration so that it does not wither or cease,
it either continues in constant succession when conditions for its destruction have not been encountered, or—
if such conditions for violation and abandonment are met— it is relinquished.
When a vow has withered and ceased and does not arise anew,
it is called "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*) or "past" (*atīta*).
However, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) depends solely upon the limits of wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*).
The non-informative [action] of the Prātimokṣa depends entirely on the limits of wholesome volitions and vows;
the non-informative [action] of non-restraint depends solely on the limits of unwholesome volitions and vows;
and the non-informative [action] of the intermediate category depends on both the limits of wholesome and unwholesome volitions and vows.
Therefore, they are now explained together.
As for the establishment [of these stages] at the level of increase,
this refers to those other than the Buddha.
Because the Buddha’s body is maintained through past karma and does not increase,
he initiates volitions (cetanā) of body and speech;
the commentary states merely that these are karma, but neither manifest (vijñapti) nor unmanifest (avijñapti).
"Name-body manifest karma" refers to the karma that manifests through bodily movement;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
It refers simply to bodily action (*kāyakarman*),
which is also the action that moves the body.
If one speaks of "bodily manifestation" (*kāyavijñapti*), [it is this].
Based on bodily intimation, speech is the karma that manifests through vocal expression;
it is also appropriately termed the karma of vocal intimation. Among the three types of volition (*cetanā*), the latter two are designated as the "path" (*mārga*) in both senses [of the term].
Regarding the preceding reflection on conduct:

among the various types of volition (*cetanā*), that which is deliberative (*vicāraṇā-cetanā*) and produces only its future fruit is designated by the single term "path" (*mārga*). Question: If it is accepted that bodily and vocal actions originated by volition are established under the name of "non-informative" (*avijñapti*), [how is this so]?
The mind also acts through volition;
it should be designated as manifest action.
[Objection: Is it not the case that bodily and vocal actions are produced by volition?

If it is granted that the name "karma" is established for volition (*cetanā*), then mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and that which is produced by volition (*cetayitvā*) should likewise be designated as "karma. Answer: This is not so.
Physical and vocal actions manifest externally to others and are thus termed "informative" (*vijñapti*);
mental action is understood solely internally by oneself and is not informative to others.
That which constitutes purposeful activity is called "karma."
The body and speech consist of volitional formations;
although the mind consists of what is induced by others,
that which is not volitional is not called karma.
Contact, mental attention, and so forth are all established as being of the three natures through the activity of volition (*cetanā*);
their essence is not itself an act of construction,
nor are they termed "karma."
Nor is it called "self-indication," because it is neither a king nor superior.
As stated in [Treatise] 59:
Body and speech are called paths of action;
the arousal of volition is called action;
and greed, hatred, and wrong view are called the paths.
This does not contradict the Sarvāstivāda school.
To summarize the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) [karma], the verse says:
"Evil, or being born into that family, Generating the resolve and giving rise to patient acceptance."
For one who possesses non-restraint, even if they take pleasure in the paths of action,
by frequently performing those deeds, they come to accomplish unwholesome karma;
so it is for others as well, such as those who have generated the resolve [for liberation] and so forth.
This [discarding of the precepts] occurs through five conditions:
the vow of renunciation, receiving the full ordination, the end of life, attaining a higher meditative absorption, and the appearance of both sexual organs.
For a bhikṣu, it does not occur through self-renunciation, because he receives [the precepts] from another after careful discernment.
The lay follower (*upāsaka*) and the one observing the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) receive [their vows] either from themselves or from another;
the manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is necessarily received from another. The non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) applies to both ways of receiving;
however, when receiving for oneself, it is solely mental, because it does not communicate to others.

One abandons the training through five conditions: taking up the life of a householder, committing a grave offense (pārājika), the disappearance of the form [of the teaching], the appearance of both sexual organs, or the severance of the roots of goodness.
One abandons it through three conditions: abandoning the homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) and the proximate cause, or the severance of the roots of goodness.
And by abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), as well as the aforementioned unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the cessation of the Dharma;
the near-dwelling (*upavāsa*) is also relinquished by three factors: the rising of the sun, the abandonment of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and the abandonment of the homogeneous class.
It is not through the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-ccheda*), nor through the cessation of the Dharma.

The discipline of concentration (samādhi-śīla) extends through the formless realms (ārūpya); the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the first [dhyāna] are called "abandoning" (prahāṇa), while those of the higher stages possess the nature of "maintaining" (dhāraṇa). This is designated as the discipline of concentration;
the discipline of the path (mārga-śīla) consists of only nine concentrations: six belonging to the form realm and three to the formless realm.
Since it is accepted that the path of seeing (darśanamārga) relies upon five stages,
the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) likewise extends only through the three formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 100, states:
The ninth stage is able to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*).
That is to say, the six stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are all able to exhaust the outflows;
this refers exclusively to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The path of seeing does not depend on the intermediate [state].

This abandonment depends on the path of seeing and the path of cultivation; it is achieved through sudden or gradual means, by the uninterrupted path, by stream-entry, or by leaping over to attain the fourth fruit.
Because there is an antidote that abandons [the defilements] within the desire realm,
the *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada), in its thirteenth chapter, states:
"The stream-enterer attains transcendence of the fourth [dhyāna] by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration."
Regarding the statement that it does not rely on other stages,
there are now two interpretations,
as explained below in the tenth fascicle.
This is based on the fact that, according to the appropriate circumstances, it is accepted that there exist minds of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) belonging to the distant stages,
up to and including the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); thus, when a mind of a different stage arises, there are both concentrated and distracted objects,
as well as objects that are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Otherwise, it would not be the case that the "discipline which follows the mind" (cittānuparivartin-śīla) is abandoned;
however, the phrase "depending on the limits of volition, aspiration, good, evil,
and so forth" is a general statement applicable to all unmanifest (avijñapti) phenomena.
This is also a distinct phrase concerning the non-manifest (avijñapti) of the Buddha-body.
The meditative precepts (dhyāna-śīla) of the Buddha-body are not different from their causes;
they differ only in that they are specifically those of liberation (prātimokṣa).
Because it does not increase.
The term "increase" in the preceding passage refers exclusively to the stage of a cause;
therefore, the Buddha’s distinct prātimokṣa-avijñapti [is not subject to such increase].
It depends solely on the limits of one's intention and vow, for it can only be relinquished when the future reaches its end; thus, it differs from [the bodhisattva precepts] based on causes.
Therefore, this first point is a distinct category of the Buddha’s precepts.

General Statement on Non-informative [Action] (avijñapti): Question: If it is accepted that bodily and vocal actions initiated by volition (cetanā) are designated as "informative" (vijñapti), then mental action, which is likewise produced by volition, should also be designated as "informative.
Answer: The nature of body and speech is karma.
One may establish the designation "informative" (*vijñapti*) based on this;
however, since intention (*cetanā*) is not itself a physical entity, how can it receive the name "informative"?
[The answer is: It is that which is produced by the volitions (*cetanā*) of body and speech.

If you grant that it is permissible to establish the designation "action" (karman) for volition (*cetanā*), then one should likewise establish the designation "action" for what is produced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Answer: Not so.
Volitional formation is called karma;
it consists of the formations of body and speech, while that of the mind,
though induced by others, is also a formation.
That which is not performed cannot be called karma.
Contact, attention, and so forth,
all establish their three natures through the performance of volition (*cetanā*).
The essence is not a conditioned production, nor is it designated as karma;
this point should be reflected upon. [The *Śāstra*] 59 states: "Body and speech are called the paths of karma."
To say that "volition" (cetanā) is karma and that "greed,
hatred, and wrong view" are the path is in accordance with the Sarvāstivāda school.
This does not contradict [the previous point].
In the *Dushasaṃprayukta* (Difficult-to-Coordinate) section,
the eighteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
All non-associated [phenomena] are conventionally existent because they possess two types of faults:
first, the fault of the cause;
second, the fault of the essence. Regarding the fault of the cause:
If that which gives rise to arising is itself called "arising," then no distinct arising of a result can be obtained. If, on the other hand,
that which is produced by arising is called "arising," [the same fault follows].
In that case, it should not be called "that which produces," and so forth,
as explained at length therein.
Now, one should raise this objection:
Regarding the third section, the refutation of attainment (*prāpti*), there are two parts:
first, the refutation of attainment;
second, the refutation of non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
There are two further points regarding the "middle":
first, simultaneous inquiry based on both scripture and reasoning,
which refers precisely to the seven difficulties.
Second, even if there were a distinct meaning to be investigated,
it would still apply to the dharmas and so forth.
Regarding the first and the middle, there are again four [points].
First, citing the scriptures to equalize the objection;
second, refuting the defense to establish that the name "Īśvara" is merely conventional;
third, showing that it can be metaphorically said to exist by virtue of its present manifestation.
Fourth, the refutation of that defense:
regarding the claim that "if there were no attainment (*prāpti*), dharmas not yet arisen would never be produced," [the response is that] present wholesome seeds and so forth must necessarily exist.
Even granting there may be other interpretations, the critique within this section consists of two parts.
First, the question regarding meditative concentration is posed;
subsequently, it is refuted individually.
Within the refutation, there are two parts.
This can be understood from the text.
Regarding the first refutation of the "ariser," there are three parts,
as shown in the text.

Regarding "accomplishment and non-accomplishment," the maturation of seeds refers to the accomplishment and non-accomplishment of those of the two vehicles and those on the worldly path; it does not speak of Bodhisattvas.
Just as for Bodhisattvas prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the two obstacles may be either present or absent,
it should be stated that for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the seeds of affliction (*kleśabīja*) may also be either present or absent; however,
the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is invariably present.
The Bodhisattva explains both:
that in the stage of equipment (sambhāra-avasthā) both are produced and not produced,
and that they are distinguished as being produced and not produced.
In the stage of application (*prayoga*), [the supernormal powers] are never accomplished.
Regarding those that are innate (*sahaja*), they may or may not be accomplished. Once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [they are accomplished].
Regarding the cultivation of the path, it may or may not be accomplished;
regarding the path of seeing, it is invariably not accomplished;
regarding the seventh [moment] of the path of cultivation, it is invariably accomplished.
The sixth [category] consists of both what is accomplished and what is not.
Regarding the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), their non-abandonment is invariably accomplished;
regarding the seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are both those that are accomplished and those that are not.
All should reflect accordingly.
Regarding the claim that the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established solely upon the seeds of the two obstructions which are defiled:
[it must be asked] whether the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not obstruct the two vehicles.
It is therefore designated as "unobscured.
For those who lack the [necessary] nature, the two obstacles do not obstruct [their practice of] the three vehicles.
Under which nature is the essence of the cognitive obstacle (jñeyāvaraṇa) subsumed?
All of these should be non-defiled. Answer: Those whose seeds can be severed and which are light—being considered not to obstruct [the path]—are termed "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).
The two types belonging to those without nature (*abhāva*) are both heavy;
as they universally obstruct the noble paths of the three vehicles, they are collectively termed "obscurations" (*nivṛta*).
If one were to designate a "worldling" (pṛthagjana) solely on the basis of possessing the seeds of conceptual discrimination,
then a single realm would become three realms; consequently,
one should be called a worldling of the three realms.
If one takes the seeds that manifest as birth,

then those who have already abandoned desire should be called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the various realms; this is because they possess the same nature as the eighth [consciousness] of an ordinary being,
and its essence is thereby obtained.
Regarding the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity),
it is briefly analyzed by way of ten sections.
First, the explanation of the name is as stated in the commentary (*śāstra*).
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, fascicle 52, states:
"The mutual similarity of various respective parts is called 'homogeneity' (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
This meaning clarifies that "group" (*nikāya*) signifies the sense of many distinct entities rather than a single one.
"Division" (bhāga) has the meaning of "category" (jāti);
"commonality" (sabhāga) has the meaning of "similarity" (sādṛśya).
Thus, the similarity among many categories is termed "homogeneous character" (nikāyasabhāga).
Second, regarding the difficulty of [the faculties] being common supports for both the manifest and the seeds:
because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established in dependence upon them, all of these are common to both;
as stated in the *Abhidharmapitaka*.
The three types of continuity—such as maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth—all apply universally.
The fifty-two [factors] indicate stages such as sound and so forth;
therefore, they apply to all three.
The four bases for the three natures apply universally;
as the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* (Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī), chapter 5, section 2, states: "Because even the Buddhas are equal regarding such categories as wrong views."
Regarding the various treatises on the five internal and external bases, those concerning only the internal [are included here];
however, because these [treatises] refute others therein,
they pertain to both the internal and the external.
Sixth, the bases for the fetters and non-fetters are all pervasive.
Seventh, regarding the total and specific bases, they are all pervasive across both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted states, whether specifically or generally.
Eighth, the bases for those abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and so forth.
Ninth, the basis for the trainings and so forth;
tenth, the general and specific acquisition and relinquishment.

Since these apply to both persons and phenomena, their respective relinquishment and acquisition should be understood according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings; now they are established by means of reasoning.
There is one that is attained but not relinquished,
namely the Buddha’s reward body (saṃbhogakāya).
There is one that is relinquished but not attained.
This refers to the state of entering the mind of nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa,
where there is a definitive acquisition and relinquishment;
that is, when sentient beings lacking the [Buddha-]nature die here and are reborn there.
There are cases where one definitely does not acquire [a dharma] and abandons it;

namely, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth. Question: Since the conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are established as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), would you also grant that the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) and "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are likewise established as provisional designations? Answer: No.
Conditioned phenomena possess a commonality (sabhāgatā) because their essence and function are similar;
however, cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not established as having a commonality because it lacks both essence and function,
and True Suchness (tathatā) is a singular entity.
Because there is no similarity,
they are not said to be of the same class (*sabhāga*).
As for the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*):
First, the abandonment through restraint (*saṃvara-prahāṇa*):
this refers to generating desire and exerting effort in order to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen.
Second, the abandonment through abandonment (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*).
Third is the cultivation of abandonment, for the purpose of preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising; and [the cultivation of realization],
for the purpose of causing unarisen wholesome states to arise.
Fourth is abandonment through protection (*ārakṣaṇā-prahāṇa*).
For the sake of maintaining already arisen wholesome dharmas, one generates desire and exerts effort;
this is because one applies oneself with all-encompassing vigor (*vīrya*).
Because wisdom itself can gradually subdue the afflictions,
it is designated by the name "right abandonment" (samyak-prahāṇa) based on its fruit;
this is the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
They are distinguished by five gates:
first, the essence;
second, the name.
Third, [the classification of] maturation and non-maturation, etc.;
fourth, [the classification of] existence and outflow-free, etc.;
fifth, the analysis through questions and answers.

If it is asked: "Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in the presence of obstacles, if it were merely a seed, why is it that in the hells all eight faculties are certain to ripen both as manifest and as seeds? Answer: Furthermore, seven faculties exist both as manifest and as seeds.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) consists solely of seeds;
since it generally refers to eight dharmas, both the manifest and the seeds are mentioned.
It is not that the life-faculty has manifest activity.
Furthermore, these eight faculties are necessarily matured;
whether they exist as seeds or as manifest activities, they are all definitely established.
This does not mean that the life-faculty also exists as a manifest activity.
Furthermore, what fault is there in taking the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) currently being maintained as the manifest [life-faculty]?
This is because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is designated by the specific functional capacity induced by karma;
the Buddha, through the power of his vows, causes the seeds to arise as the manifest.
Even the demarcation between matter and mind, and so forth, is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Question: When one enters the mindless state through aversion to the mind, there is a subtle mind;
when one enters the formless state through aversion to matter, there is subtle matter.

Question: One who is weary of the body enters the state of being bodiless, yet possesses a subtle body. Answer: If one is weary of the coarse body, there is also a subtle body, as in the case of the Buddha-body.
When both the coarse and the subtle are entirely weary of, one no longer possesses a body.
Because it is distinct from the mind: Question—One enters the mindless state through aversion toward the mind;
these two meditative attainments (samāpatti) are called "mindless.
Through aversion toward the first, one enters the second.
"The second dhyāna is called 'mindless'. Answer: "One who is weary of the mind is weary of all six [consciousnesses].
The two meditative attainments (samāpatti) are called 'mindless.
One is weary of the lower [levels], not of the higher mind."
The higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) are not without mind. Question:

One who is weary of the eight formless [attainments] (*ārūpya*)—even though there is subtle form (*rūpa*) present, they are called "formless"—enters the higher attainments from below out of weariness.
The higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are called "mindless" because the karma-produced matter (karmaja-rūpa) does not exist in the higher realms;
although subtle matter exists there and is thus called "formless" (ārūpya),
the retributive mind (vipākacitta) does exist in the higher realms.
It cannot be called "mindless. Question: The seed of mind guards against the mind;
the essence of meditative concentration is neither mind nor form.
The seed of form guards against form.
Question: The essence of the precepts (*śīla*) is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*). Answer: That which is prevented (*nivārya*) is by nature form;
that which prevents (*nivāraka*) is likewise included within form. Question:

If that which is loathed (*vidveṣya*) is the mind, then that which loathes (*vidviṣṭa*) should be subsumed under the mind. Answer: Both that which is prevented and that which is produced [by it] are form.
That which can prevent form is also called form;
though that which is to be loathed is the mind, it does not give rise to anything [further].
That which can prevent the mind is neither mind nor form. Question: This may be so for dispersed forms.

Regarding the question: "How can one name and form that which is unarisen through the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration and the Path?"—one should apply diligent investigation to this difficult point.
Answer: It is the mind of revulsion; it is revulsion toward all things.
One can cultivate revulsion toward that which is non-material (arūpa), whereas the mind [itself] cannot.
Regarding the prevention of form (rūpa), it prevents only evil;
because it is capable of such prevention, it is called "form. Question: Does the mind that cultivates revulsion apply to all things?
One who is able to weary of the seeds of mind-only, and who guards against form—guarding only against evil—is able to guard against what should manifest. Answer: This applies to all.
In the second fascicle, the Sthavira school establishes two characteristics,
while the Mahīśāsaka school establishes three:
first, the momentary destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*).
All matter and mind constitute the two aggregates of one period,
namely, the life-span.
These two distinguish the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena].
Third, the aggregates that exhaust saṃsāra, though distinct dharmas, do not constitute the characteristics themselves. The Saṃmitīya school establishes four characteristics.
Material phenomena (rūpadharma) undergo arising and ceasing over a long duration of one life-span;
whereas mind, mental factors, lamp flames, and bell sounds arise and cease moment by moment (kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa).
Movements and the like endure for a longer period of time.
The *Mahāpṛthivī-sūtra* states that the earth remains for an eon (*kalpa*). If the Sautrāntikas follow the Sarvāstivādins,
then as stated in the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*,
their intention is that mental activity arises from the future.
The three characteristics function in the present;
however, they are merely provisional designations and not the fundamental tenets.
The characteristics originally maintained by the Sautrāntika masters are the same as those in the Mahāyāna;
whereas the ancient Sarvāstivādins held that [dharmas] exist in the future.
In the present, there is a distinction between the three phases within a single moment;
the initial stage is called "abiding" (sthiti),
and it is this that is capable of grasping the fruit.
Because there exists a superior method, [the other] two—
alteration and cessation— are unable [to do so],
for their power is weak.
The stage following abiding, which causes the dharma to decline, is called the stage of change (*anyathātva*).
The stage following change, which renders the dharma incapable of further function, is called cessation (*nirodha*). This is according to the Vaibhāṣikas.
Arising occurs in the future;
it functions simultaneously with the three [marks] of duration, change, and cessation.
Arising causes a dharma to be about to become functional.
Stability (sthiti) causes a dharma to grasp its future fruit and arise;
at the very moment of stability,
change (jarā) causes the dharma to be unable to reach what it previously was, making it weaker than before.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are by their very nature weak in power and cannot reach as far as the preceding ones,
yet there are times when a phenomenon increases;
this occurs because other conditions arrive and cause it to arise.
In this way, it is not the fundamental nature of the dharma;
for if the fundamental nature were inferior, it would necessarily undergo decay and change.
At the time of its growth, that very change remains within the substance of the nature itself.
Because it causes the dharma to become inferior;

cessation exerts its function precisely at the time of abiding, causing that function to reach the subsequent moment. If the Sūtra speaks of only two characteristics, the masters who maintain that all conditioned phenomena exist (Sarvāstivādins) say:
By citing the initial and final characteristics, the intermediate stages are abbreviated.
This transformation of arising renders phenomena functional;
the time when they are functional is the present.
Because at the time of future arising, a phenomenon has not yet served its function;
cessation can cause a phenomenon to become about to lose its function,
since it is truly without function during the subsequent moment.
Although the characteristic of duration exists, it does not reach [the state of] arising;
although the characteristic of change exists, it does not reach [the state of] cessation.
Therefore, duration and change are abbreviated.
Regarding the statement that it "only speaks of arising and ceasing," the Master of Correct Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) says:
"This reveals the manifestation of activity at two times:
in the future, it manifests the functional capacity for arising."
It causes dharmas to enter the present;
when there is the time of cessation in the present,
it causes dharmas to enter the past.
The functions of subsistence (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*) are simultaneous with cessation (*nirodha*);
because their timing is not distinct, they are not mentioned separately.
Birth (*jāti*) and cessation (*nirodha*), however, mark the beginning of the states of being functional and non-functional.
It does not state that arising, abiding, and change constitute two functions, etc.
Regarding the third [section], the refutation of the four characteristics, there are two parts.
First is the general negation.
It will be refuted separately later.
Within the separate refutations, there are seven:
first, the objection that the sixfold transformation is without distinction.
Second is the objection that the subject and object are not distinct.
Both of these [arguments] possess the fallacies of a reason (*hetu*) that contradicts the proponent's own tenet (*siddhānta-viruddha*) and a reason that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the first, their formal inference (*prayoga*) states:
Regarding the three characteristics of the conditioned:
the characteristic must have a distinct substantial entity separate from the characterized dharma,
because it is expressed as a term denoting possession.
As with the robe of Devadatta,
the subsequent inference states that the three bodies constitute the characteristic mark.
The characterized phenomenon (lakṣya) must necessarily have a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because it is that which is characterized (lakṣaṇa),
just like smoke and other such signs.
Therefore, both [positions] entail two faults.
First, there is the difficulty of contradiction with inference (*anumāna-virodha*).
You [assert that] names, phrases, and phonemes...

It is not a real designator, because it is admitted to be distinct from sound, like color, fragrance, and so forth. Second, [the author] concludes by attributing designation to sound. Third, the opponent offers this defense:
The name and so forth upon sound are neither identical to nor different from sound.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: "The inflections upon sound [are neither identical to nor different from it]."
The distinctness of the basis must exist as a real entity,
because it is a curvature within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
just like length, shortness, and so forth.
This involves three fallacies.
First, there is the deficiency of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*),
because [the argument] does not differentiate between the length of this and that.
Second, if the length and so forth of a Mahāyāna [sūtra] are used as the analogy,
there is no fault of the probandum being absent in the homologous instance (*sapakṣa*),
because the length and so forth of the Mahāyāna are not substantially real entities distinct from their substratum.
Third, if one uses "one's own growth" and so forth as an analogy,
there is the fault of contradicting the existence of that specific characteristic within the cause;
for [growth] exists in a real entity distinct from its substratum.

The distinctions between phenomena consist in such things as "substantially existing with a different basis in a different location" and "substantially existing with a different basis in the same location."
The Pramāṇa states:
"The curvature in sound is certainly not different from the curvature in the real aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) existing in a distinct location that serves as its basis."
Just as with long and short,
or with letters and so forth,
they are not distinct because they are subsumed within their respective locations.
Therefore, it is known that names and so forth are in fact useless. Fourth, the external objection states:
"Internal sounds are merely convoluted;
they cannot express or signify."
Because sound is characterized by curvature (or articulation),
like the sound of strings or pipes;
the Master of the Treatise [Dignāga] establishes this as a contradiction regarding the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*).
Internal sound is tortuous;
it can produce names and cannot produce names,
because it is a distinction among existing phenomena (*dharma*).
The Pramāṇa states:
"The internal sound is tortuous;
it cannot produce names."
Because sound is subject to distortion,
like the sound of strings or pipes;
this is an objection raised from the perspective of another school.
Furthermore, who says that they [the opponents] would state their own tenets for fear of contradicting inference?
The *Pramāṇa* states:
"Sounds such as those of strings, pipes, and wind instruments are capable of expressing [meaning]."
This is because there is a deviation regarding the great sound due to its being a derivative [of sound].
For example, regarding the internal sound that you yourself accept, their formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
"The Mahāyāna, the wind, the sound of a bell, and so forth..."
It must possess the function of signification,
because its nature is that of sound,
just like internal vocal sounds and the like.
Alternatively, internal sounds and so forth cannot be expressed [by words],
because they are subsumed under the category of sound.
Regarding the wind-bells and so forth, it is said next that [the case] is directly resolved by means of reasoning:
just as those wind-bells do not produce names and the like,
my sounds of wind and so forth likewise cannot express or measure [anything].
The sounds of your wind-bells and the like should give rise to names,
because they are subsumed under the category of sound.
Just as with internal vocal sounds, the fifth [type], contentious speech, differs from sound.
As for the term "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ-priya*),
in Sanskrit it is *mūrkha*.
This is called "foolish.
There are three names for a fool:
first, *deva*, which in Chinese is translated as "heaven" (*tian*).
Second, Nibhū, pronounced with a level tone; this is translated as "Radiance.
Third, Parajāpati; this is translated as "Lord of Beings.
*Parā* means "beings."
*Patidhī* means "mistress";
it was formerly translated as "Mistress of the World.
*Mahāprajāpatī* means "Great Mistress of Beings" (*Dàshēngzhǔ*). This is who she is.
This refers to the Brahmā King. Among those superior in the world, none surpass the gods;
among those inferior in the world, none surpass the fool.
This is because the fool is addressed as "god" for the purpose of disciplining him.
"Calling slaves 'young masters' and so forth": "Luminosity" (prabhāsvara) means the sense of clear illumination.
Fools, being shrouded in the darkness of delusion, mistakenly call it luminosity.
It is like calling a poor person wealthy or a dull-witted person intelligent; likewise,
the Brahmā King is universally regarded by the world as a father.
Just as that which has arisen merely knows how to sit upright,
and although it can produce everything, it performs no action at all—
the fool is likened to that.
Although they are driven to perform a hundred kinds of tasks,
they possess no knowledge at all;
they lack even the slightest discernment.
The inferior is designated by the name of the superior, thus called "Lord of Beings" (Prajāpati).
This foolish man is pitiable, and for this reason he is called "Beloved of the Gods" (Devānāmpriya).
The remaining meanings are as usual.
Question: A syllable (*akṣara*) is the basis for names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), yet it does not itself express meaning.
Since in the Mahāyāna there is no essence apart from sound, what constitutes a syllable?
In this land [of China], there is only that which is called a single character (*zi*).
Its characters are difficult to understand;
for the most part, that region lacks even a single named character.
For example, the word for "killing" is composed of three characters combined.
That is to say, the three syllables *sha*, *ṭa*, and *ta* combined form the single term "killing" (*saṭṭha*).
The character *u* (𠍜) has a sound like that of a cloud;
because it lacks any denotative meaning, it is not expressed.

Therefore, although these are established as provisional, they still possess the turning of syllables (*vyañjana*) and the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*).
The body of syllables is distinct from the body of names.
"Syllable" (*vyañjana*) means that which manifests meaning.
Because it manifests those two,
it is also called "manifestation" (nirukti);
for it serves as the basis by which their meaning is made manifest.
Furthermore, names do not undergo transformation into something else,
such as the words *yǎn* (咽) or *yē* (噎),
as explained in the commentary regarding distinct names and so forth.
Regarding "name-body" (*nāmakāya*): "name" (*nāman*) refers to that which calls out;
it is called a "name" because it is the cause for designation.
"Phrase" (*pada*) is, in Sanskrit, *padam*.
As explained in the commentary, it should be stated as "traces" (*pada*).
Regarding the term "name" (*nāman*), [the compounds] such as "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.
"Body" (*kāya*) is a collective term for the two [i.e., name and phrase].
A "name" (nāma) refers to a single distinct designation;
a collection of such distinct names is called a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
A collection of two or more names is termed a "body" (kāya).
Therefore, it is likewise with the body that has many names;
for a single name is not the body.
This is not a *karmadhāraya* compound;
however, these three types are not referred to by the term "name" (*nāman*) alone.
Furthermore, it does not mention "name-groups" (nāmakāya) by name;
rather, it refers only to "name-groups" and so forth because these terms encompass both the concise and the extensive.
To speak briefly of the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*) by way of summary—since "many" implies being extensive—the second [section] distinguishes its specific characteristics.
The treatise states: "Names signify their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth."
The fifty-second [fascicle] states:
"The phoneme (*akṣara*) should be understood as the basis for names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*),
with respect to all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and all referents (*abhidheya*)."
The most abbreviated characteristic is a syllable;
if intermediate, it is a name;
if extensive, it is a phrase.
If one understands only the phonetic tones based on the literal text,
one cannot understand all the meanings of the phenomena;
this is the case if one relies merely upon names.
Furthermore, they are able to comprehend the intrinsic nature of those phenomena and also understand their phonetic expressions; however,
they are unable to comprehend the profound and vast distinctions among the phenomena that have been analyzed.
If one relies on the general definition, all [factors] can be understood;
the Abhidharma is likewise.
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Exposition of the Teachings), fascicle 12, states:
There are syllables that are not names,
namely a single syllable.
There are names that are not phrases.
That is to say, there is the name consisting of a single syllable;
a phrase necessarily consists of names,

Question: The seventh [consciousness], in which images are subsumed within the seeing-nature (*darśana-bhāga*), may be termed "obscured" (*nivṛta*);
however, in which images are subsumed within the object-substance (*nimitta-bhāga*), it may be termed "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).
Likewise, one should subsume the characteristic (nimitta) into the seeing (darśana) and name it "discrimination" (vikalpa);

one should subsume the reflection (pratibimba) into the substance (bimba) and name it "maturation" (vipāka). Answer: Because they are not separate from the seeing, their nature and category may be the same.
That which is not a cognitive faculty (ālambaka) is not termed "discrimination" (vikalpa).
Since it arises by depending upon a material substrate (dravya), it may be classified as non-obscured (anivṛta);
however, because it is neither karma nor its fruit, it is not classified as maturation (vipāka). Question: That which is not a cognitive faculty does not follow from discrimination.
The obscured [unwholesome] should be understood in the same way.
It is not that it is not a result of karma because it does not arise from maturation (*vipāka*).
The unobscured [neutral] should likewise be so. Answer: Its nature permeates many dharmas.
The two natures can be abandoned through seeing;
as for the meaning of "fruit," it is restricted to not being abandoned through cultivation, nor through conceptualization, nor through synonyms, nor as maturation (*vipāka*).
This is because these two types of dharma-grasping are coarse and thus easily severed.
From the time of entering the first stage until its final cessation,
there are four kinds at the beginning.
First is the stage (*bhūmi*).
First, it is abandoned in the first stage (*bhūmi*) and not in other stages.
Second, it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and not by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because within that [first stage], there is only seeing and no cultivation.
The three aspects of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
First, because this occurs in the path of true seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and not in the path of subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna-mārga*).
Fourth, the four paths.
This is because, at the beginning, one is in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and not yet in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is based on the view that the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) occurs within a single moment of mind;
it is not an explanation based on the abandonment of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).
In these four [stages], first one abandons the conceptual attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
If the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) abandons the heavy residues (*dausthulya*),
this occurs during the three moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.
This should be explained according to the meaning:
delusion regarding the shallow necessarily involves the deep; human attachment necessarily involves dharmas.
Understanding the shallow does not involve the deep; the emptiness of persons does not involve dharmas.
When awakening is profound, it must be shallow regarding the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), yet there is still the existence of a person (pudgala).
When delusion is profound, it is likewise shallow regarding both phenomena and persons;
nevertheless, the person is necessarily constant and unitary.
There are phenomena that do not inherently possess a person;
yet when a person employs them, they necessarily involve a substantial entity.
Thus, the person clings to these phenomena as being definitively existent.
The statement that "the function of conditions must depend upon a substantially existent essence" is based on correct reasoning;
it does not refer to the tenets held by non-Buddhists or the Hīnayāna schools.
Since its substance is not non-existent, it can function as a condition and thus possesses the status of being an object of cognition (*sālambana*). This is because,
as established in the previous fascicle, the Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist.
Even if the meaning of "condition" were established, there would be no object of cognition (*ālambana*);
this [position] is not accepted by us in terms of *parārthānumāna* (inference for others).

Since we are now stating the correct principle, there is no contradiction. It is our own position that the mental factors (*caitta*) within the same aggregate (*nikāya-sabhāga*) take one another as objects.
The eighth fascicle below states: "Do not see [the object] as having a different substance from the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
This is intended to preclude the fault of the object being of a different substance from the seeing-part;
it does not mean to inform us that the objective support must necessarily be the same as the seeing-part.

The Buddha’s eighth [consciousness], the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth, shares the same object of cognition as the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), because it is their own seeing-part;
therefore, there is no contradiction. Question: Since the mind and mental factors are already mutually associated, why is this further explained?
Since the various self-witnessing portions (svasaṃvedanabhāga) do not have the same object,
and their objects are not similar either,
how can they be said to be associated (saṃprayukta)?
The same applies to the question regarding the self-cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti*).
Since self-cognition is the very essence of consciousness, how could it not be associated [with mental factors]? It possesses [the factors of] time, basis, object, and location.
Regarding these points of deficiency and so forth:
since each takes its own view as the object and not that of another,
this matter should be reflected upon.
"If my doctrine has no basis, why resort to provisional designations?
Since that which is being compared does not exist, who could be the one performing the comparison?
Because the provisional designation of the "comparer" does not exist, [the doctrine is established].
The semblance of commonality is also not established;
for it cannot be understood as a distinct meaning based on a conventional designation such as "substance" (svabhāva),
since both the worldly and the scriptural [perspectives] fail to establish such a semblance.
The refutation of the true reality of the Hīnayāna consists of three parts:
first, a general negation;
second, a detailed exposition.
Next is the conclusion regarding the basis.
This is further divided into three parts.
First, it is shown that [the mind] does not rely on the ultimate reality, but functions solely in dependence upon common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Next, it is shown that the wisdom which expresses [these] possesses a superior function,
nor is it something apart from these. Finally,
it is generally established that conventional designations do not depend upon real entities.
However, since conventional cognition and linguistic expression necessarily arise based on sound and so forth, this [passage] concludes that they depend solely on what follows.
As stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
If both the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the objects are what are known by the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
how are these two types of valid cognition established based on the two characteristics?
One interpretation holds that the two types of valid cognition are established based on the two characteristics while in a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
It does not speak of a fixed state;
if the concentrated mind takes all marks as its object,
they are all subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There is an interpretation that the concentrated mind takes only specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object;
however, when it is induced by the skillful means of common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) to take as its object the principles manifested by those common characteristics,
this is spoken of from the perspective of those skillful means.
That which is not thus is called knowing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
By this principle,
it is said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, termed emptiness and selflessness.
Some say that suchness, as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, is not a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
According to the true meaning, however,
its two characteristics differ slightly from those in the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).
All the actual meanings contained within those teachings are termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This is because the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena each adhere to their own essence and do not share it with others.
If the conceptualizing mind establishes a single category such that both the signifier and the signified pervade all phenomena—
like a thread threading through flowers, termed the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
This essential [distinction] is conceptually established through the discrimination of the distracted mind;
it is the object of inference (*anumāna*).
All states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that are free from such discrimination are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Although [these characteristics] take various phenomena such as suffering and impermanence as their objects,
they are each called "specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa) because they exist individually within each phenomenon.
Although true thusness (tathatā) is manifested as a "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), [it is nonetheless distinct].
Because these dharmas possess their own actual nature and because they possess their own individual nature,
they are not common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
One cannot designate them as common characteristics simply because they are neither identical to nor different from all other dharmas.
Because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is neither identical to nor different from all general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
that treatise states that whatever real meaning exists upon all phenomena is called the specific characteristic.
Since the meaning of the sūtra is not thus, there is no contradiction;
nor is there any other expedient means apart from this.
There are two interpretations.
One interpretation states that conventional cognition itself, which designates the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as a conceptual construct, serves as the basis for that conventionality.
This is because conventional cognition reveals and expresses phenomena,
just as a finger points toward the moon.
If it were not so, how could one say that the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is that which is realized?
Second, conventional cognition (prajñapti-jñāna) cannot express an object as its specific characteristic;
nor is there any other means apart from these two by which a specific characteristic could be provisionally established to serve as the basis for conventionality.
This demonstrates that since these two cannot be apprehended by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
there is no other means apart from this by which their own-characteristic can be apprehended;
the intent is to show that, apart from realized wisdom (*pramāṇajñāna*), nothing else is capable of apprehending the own-characteristic.
Forty-nine [stages] are established as seven grounds:
first, the stage of the nature-type;
second, the stage of practice through resolute belief.
3. The stage of the purified and superior mind at rest;
4. The stage of practicing correct conduct;
5. The stage of certainty.
Sixth, the stage of definitive practice;

seventh, the stage of reaching the ultimate. [These comprise] the forty-seven types: the lineage, the stage of conduct through aspiration, the stage of supreme joy, the stage of superior ethical discipline, the stage of superior mind, the three stages of wisdom, the stage of the factors of enlightenment, the stage of dependent origination, the stage of signlessness with effort, the stage of signlessness without effort, the stage of unhindered analytical knowledge, the supreme bodhisattva stage, and the ultimate tathāgata stage.
The stage of lineage (*gotrabhūmi*) is the position of lineage.
The stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) is the position of conduct through resolute belief.

The stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi*) is the stage of the practice of the Joyful One (*pramuditācaryā*). The stage of correct practice (*samyakpratipattibhūmi*) is the stage of higher affliction (*adhiprajñā*).
The higher mind;
the three kinds of higher wisdom;
and the dwelling in signlessness with applied effort and exertion.

The stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*) is precisely the dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*) that is without application (*anabhisamskāra*) and without effort (*anābhoga*). There are three kinds of certainty:
first, certainty of lineage (*gotra-niyama*);
second, certainty of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda-niyama*).
Third is the certainty of non-erroneous practice.
Because the Bodhisattvas on this stage have entered the third certainty,
the stage of certain practice is the dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Upon reaching the ultimate stage, one is established as a most excellently perfected bodhisattva and a Tathāgata-abiding.
The name *ālaya* applies to the first four stages;
the name *vipāka* extends through six and a half stages,
because the seventh stage includes the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
The name ādāna-vijñāna penetrates through the seven stages;
however, in the state of defilement,
it is for the most part maturation (vipāka).
Because it penetrates the ālayavijñāna; furthermore, regarding the thirteen abodes:
the first is called "penetrating nine," and the third is called "penetrating thirteen."
The term "ripening" (*vipāka*) refers to twelve [factors];
thus, it is called "many.
Because it is designated based on birth and death (*saṃsāra*), only these are taken.
Regarding these two interpretations based on uncommon objects of focus, which take the three natures as their objects,
the two vehicles are not mentioned; however,
those of the two vehicles who turn toward [the Mahāyāna] are also included herein.
The second part of the commentary explains the interpretation common to the three vehicles.
The above serves to distinguish its own specific name;
it must be that which is not designated as "mind."
This is because it is equal in name to the *ālayavijñāna*;
since the name "mind" (*manas*) does not apply to the seventh [consciousness], it is not taken [as such].
Furthermore, it serves to distinguish it from other consciousnesses.
"Much" (*bahu*) has the meaning of continuity.
That which operates at all times is called "much," because it operates for a long duration.
"Vipāka" refers to the fruit of karma;
specifically, it is the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) among the five fruits.
Although the six consciousnesses possess ripening, they do not constitute many [distinct ripening fruits].
Although the seventh [consciousness] is manifold, it is not a maturation;
therefore, this name applies exclusively to it.
Furthermore, "manifold" (bahu) carries the sense of being extensive.
This is the general meaning.
Although the sense of "maturation" (*vipāka*) applies to all six consciousnesses,
the name is not established as plural unless it refers to the primary subject of the collective retribution.
The seventh [consciousness] is neither manifold nor a maturation;
therefore it is called "maturation," while other consciousnesses are not so named.
Furthermore, as for that which "reflects" (cintana):
The [text] distinguishes it from other consciousnesses as explained in the commentary.
Furthermore, it distinguishes it from itself. Why is this called "manas" (mind)? There are two meanings:
first, it is called "manas" in the sense of being a support (*āśraya*).

Second, that which deliberates is called *manas*. Why is it termed "deliberation" (*santīraṇa*) and not "basis" (*āśraya*)? Because the designation "basis" is shared with others [the sense-faculties], whereas this [designation] is not shared.
Furthermore, the term "basis" (āśraya) implies both the other [the supported] and manifests itself [the supporter],
because it manifests the supported by means of the supporter.
The term "cognition" (manana) signifies the meaning of its own intrinsic characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
The essence is manifested through its activity.
Because its objects are manifold, it arises in a continuous succession.
When its mode of activity and its objects are remote, it is termed "deliberate."
Therefore, because it manifests its own nature through the aspect of deliberation (*santīraṇa*), it is not called a support (*āśraya*).
Furthermore, that which is currently engaged in deliberation is termed "mind" (*manas*).
According to the second [chapter] of the Abhidharma, the meaning of immediate cognition (*anantarajñāna*) is mind.
That is, the faculties are extinguished in succession.
This present deliberation is "presently deliberating";
it is called "constant" (*nitya*) to distinguish it from that which is uninterrupted (*anantara*).
This is to reveal that this deliberation is constantly present. Furthermore, it distinguishes it from its own name.
Why is it not called "mind" (*citta*) or "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), but is uniquely called "intellect" (*manas*)?
As the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* and other texts state, consciousness is of eight kinds.

Some maintain that all eight [consciousnesses] are called "mind" (*citta*) because they possess the nature of accumulating; however, since the meaning of "constant and thorough deliberation" (*nitya-paricchedana*) is predominant in the eighth consciousness, it alone is designated as "mind.
If "mind" were defined merely by the sense of constant accumulation, it would not apply to the eighth consciousness.
If one understands that "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the cognition of objects,
it does not apply to the other six [bases].
Therefore, they are designated individually as "mind" (manas), and the term "citta" or "vijñāna" is not used for them.
By this, two meanings are excluded regarding other consciousnesses:
because these other consciousnesses are neither constant nor discerning.
As explained in the commentary:

secondly, among these, the mind (*manas*)—unlike the [five] consciousnesses which do not reach eight or six [objects]—is superior to the consciousnesses in its constant function of self-reflexive cogitation (*manana*). Thus, it is distinguished by its own name. Furthermore, within this [explanation of its] own name, there are also two [aspects].
First, it does not rely solely on the meaning of "understanding" (*jñāna*);
for among the various treatises, the term "reliance" (*niśraya*) is not applied to the sense of "practice" (*caryā*).
Second, it reveals that [the Buddha] is eternally present, rather than being a consciousness that arises without interruption.
Furthermore, regarding that which cognizes objects:
first, there is that which manifests its own essence solely through the aspect of the mode of seeing.
Second, distinguishing it from other consciousnesses has four points.
First, because it is easily known by all.
First, those such as infants and the like all know that there is a cause;
second, both [parties] agree that there is a cause;
third, it is universally accepted by the three vehicles.
Third, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse;
fourth, because their objects (*ālambana*) are coarse.
Only these six are called "cognizing objects" (*vijñapti*), while the others do not receive that name. Furthermore, they may themselves be termed "mind" (*citta*) or "mentality" (*manas*).

Why is it called only "vijñāna" (consciousness) and not "citta" (mind), "manas" (intellect), and so forth? Because its mode of activity in cognizing objects is coarse, it is easy to understand; thus its own nature is made manifest.
This is not the case for citta and manas.
Because the meaning of the term "mind" (*citta*) as applied to visual consciousness and the rest is difficult to understand,
the section on the "Mind Ground" (*cittabhūmi*) states that all eight are called "mind."
The Abhidharma and other treatises speak of "immediately preceding awakening" (*anantarya-bodhi-citta*);
therefore, it is distinguished by its specific name.
Furthermore, it is distinguished from those not so named, such as "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "manifestation" (*samudācāra*).
Because the definitions and characteristics of terms such as "maturation" (*vipāka*) are difficult to understand,
and because they are for the most part not applicable [to this context],
other specific meanings are explained in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* (Dapifa chao) and in separate chapters.
The essence and characteristics, being submerged and hidden, are termed the "cause";
therefore, they exist solely within the seeds.
The manifestation of essence and function is established as the "fruit."
Because it is designated as "seeing," it does not reside within the seeds;
otherwise, it would necessarily pervade both cause and fruit.
Within the capacity for transformation, there are two sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
First, one should formulate a statement concerning cause and effect in general.
Next, one should formulate statements concerning the respective causes and effects of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and maturation (*vipāka*).
Finally, one should formulate statements by correlating these two pairs.
Regarding subsequent transformation (*pariṇāma*), it manifests as phrases.
One should contemplate this by combining them into five sets of four phrases.
There are cases where there is only transformation (*pariṇāma*) which is termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), but not manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) which is termed "transformation."
This refers to all seeds.
There are those that merely manifest and are thus called "transformation" (pariṇāma) rather than "evolution" (pariṇāma);
these refer to the manifestation of the karmic fruits within the eighth consciousness and the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, regarding all minds and mental factors associated with the Buddha’s merits,
those that possess the category of "simultaneous occurrence" (sahabhū) are said to have the seven consciousnesses as their cause.
Regarding that which is neither [of the two]:
this refers to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of the maturation consciousness (vipākavijñāna), for it is merely that which has been transformed.
Because all factors at the stage of the cause possess the characteristic of power and function as perfumers (*vāsanā*),
they are termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) in the sense of undergoing transformation; they are not termed "transformation" in the sense of manifesting through transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
It is subsumed under the first phrase:
the objective-image portions (nimitta-bhāga) of the karma-results of the six consciousnesses within their causal state,
as well as all [aspects] of the eighth [consciousness].
The various minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) of the Buddha-fruit, along with their objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga), all constitute the fourth category.
Furthermore, there are those that undergo transformation due to causes but not due to the fruit;
these refer to all conditioned uncontaminated seeds (anāsrava-bīja) from the time one has already attained Buddhahood onward.
Because the Buddha has no further manifestation produced by perfuming,
there is transformation of the fruit but not transformation of the cause;
that is to say, the karmic fruits within the eighth consciousness and the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s manifestation of all minds and mental factors":
this refers to the seven consciousnesses acting as perfumers (*vāsana*) for the active states (*pravṛtti*) and as producers of seeds (*bīja*).
Regarding "neither":

this refers to all objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) within the state of Buddhahood. These are transformed by the causal capacity [of consciousness] solely as outflow-causes (*niṣyanda-hetu*). Regarding the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*):
afflictions (*kleśa*) are exclusively outflow-causes and are not transformations of effects.
The fruit of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) natural seed (*dharmatā-bīja*).
There are those that are exclusively results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and not results of transformation through causes.
This means that when the fruit of Buddhahood manifests as the eight consciousnesses,
there is a state of coexistence;
that is, the seventh and sixth consciousnesses are untainted (anāsrava) due to their causes.

Furthermore, regarding the seeds that serve as the causes for majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), craftsmanship (*śilpa*), and transformations (*nirmāṇa*), there is a category that is neither [of these].

This refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the Buddha-fruit. Within the fourfold logical set (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning the transformation that takes maturation (*vipāka*) as its cause and fruit, [the Buddha-fruit] is established as such.
There are only three propositions,
for there is no third proposition.
The first proposition consists of the seeds of contaminated wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas].
The eighth consciousness and the sixth consciousness manifest as the fruits of karma; seeds constitute the second phrase.
There is no third phrase.
That which is neither should be understood according to reason.
The various textual categories and verses should all be explained separately.
Regarding the seventh and sixth consciousnesses— which are neither virtuous nor non-virtuous and include the mind of karmic fruition and so forth—
these constitute five phrases for each of the eight consciousnesses.
This shall be considered separately later.
True maturation possesses three characteristics.
First, it is the fruit of a single karma;
second, it is uninterrupted;
third, it pervades the three realms.
The seventh possesses the latter two meanings but not the first;
the sixth, the retributive mind (*vipākacitta*), possesses the first and the last meanings but not the middle;
and the non-retributive mind possesses the last one meaning but not the first two.
The five sensory consciousnesses and the retributive mind possess the first [of the three meanings] but not the latter two;
the non-retributive mind lacks all three meanings.
Therefore, only the eighth consciousness alone receives this name.
Among the ten causes, how many causes can the eighth, manifest activity (*samudācāra*), serve with respect to all phenomena?
First, the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*); second, the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*).
(1) By way of function, (2) by way of basis, and (3) by way of mutual inclusion;
(3) they share a common purpose,
and (4) they are non-contradictory.
It is not by way of verbal expression;
it is not by way of moistening, because it does not produce subsequent fruits that have not yet been moistened;
and it is not by way of inducing, because of their fixed distinctness.
It does not directly induce the arising of another,
nor is it necessarily a distinct arising;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
This can be understood through reflection.
With respect to all phenomena, the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) can function as eight causes:

the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*), the cause of attraction (*ākṣepa-hetu*), the cause of production (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), the cause of sustenance (*parigraha-hetu*), the cause of projection (*āvāhaka-hetu*), the cause of distinctness (*pratiniyama-hetu*), the cause of cooperation (*sahakāri-hetu*), and the cause of non-contradiction (*avirodha-hetu*).
There are only two types [of contradiction]: that which contradicts conventional designation and that which contradicts reality.
According to this, it is said that all three characteristics exist solely as active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Because it is presently visible;
because its grasping is preeminent;
and because it takes that preeminence as its characteristic—these are the three characteristics of the eighth [consciousness].
The second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that seeds serve as the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
Manifest activity is the characteristic of the fruit,
because it is produced from two kinds [of causes].
Both manifest activity and seeds are the self-characteristic.
Because both the manifest and the seeds constitute its own essence, and because it is taught that only the manifest [activity] is what is stored,
and the locus of storage is called the "storehouse" (ālaya)—

such is the intended meaning of the root text of the treatise. Furthermore, by explaining the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is shown that the eighth consciousness is the storehouse for both the manifest activity and all seeds.
The self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is pervasive,
because all aspects (*sarvākāra*) must be further distinguished.
The causal characteristic (*hetulakṣaṇa*) is also pervasive.
The characteristics of its fruit consist solely of the eighth consciousness in its manifest and seed states;
other seeds are excluded because they are not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). This is stated in the fourth [chapter].
The three characteristics (trilakṣaṇa) both include the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and all modes (*sarvākāra*),
because they serve as mutual cause and effect with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
As the *Saṃgrahaṇī* states:
Regarding the statement that all phenomena produced by perfuming arise from them:
because these [phenomena] and those [seeds] act as mutual conditions for the maturation-consciousness and the evolving consciousnesses,
their resultant characteristics are likewise pervasive.

Furthermore, all dharmas reside within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the consciousness likewise resides within them; thus, they exist as causes endowed with the three characteristics.
The fruit of Buddhahood, however, consists solely of its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and causal characteristic (hetulakṣaṇa).
It lacks the characteristic of being a fruit,
because it is neither perfumed nor a maturation (*vipāka*).
If one follows the verse of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
It is not only maturation that is termed "fruit-characteristic";
rather, whatever arises from another is termed "fruit-characteristic.
Thus, the manifest activity of the Buddha-fruit may also be called "fruit-characteristic."
Because it arises from its own seeds,
the former interpretation is superior;
