Regarding the statement that first the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) transform and subsequently derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) arises,
as well as the passage concerning "being bound by the same [realm]" and so forth:

one interpretation holds that this teaching refers to the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*) within the stages of both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Because it possesses a body as its basis,
the matter that is the fruit of the formless attainments is produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the essential nature.
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are no primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because there is no body to serve as their support.

Regarding the statement that the realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and self or other within such concentrations are not fixed: this refers to the fact that these factors are variable depending on the specific state of concentration.
This consists of five [factors]:
first, the power of meditative concentration;
second, the power of supernormal faculties.
Third, the power of the roots of goodness;
fourth, the power of borrowed consciousness;
fifth, the power of great vows.
Due to the practice of great vows, the form of other stages is induced to manifest before one.
However, the eighth consciousness possesses only the first two types;
later, it also extends to the others.
This is revealed incidentally,
and there is no fault in doing so;
it is like the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mental faculty (*manas*) of the eighth consciousness inducing the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
It causes the eighth transformation of the desire realm;
it does not preclude the existence of seeds of form resulting from meditative concentration within the desire realm,
yet there is no capacity to induce such a transformation, just as in the case of the eighth consciousness when it takes an object.
Do the [minds] take as their object the conventional matter (prajñaptirūpa) within visible forms, sounds, and tangibles?
If they do, why do they not take as their object the conventional matter of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?

This objection applies to the spontaneous mind and the eight associated mental factors. Seeing arises from the seeds of its own meditative concentration; this is called transformation by way of the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
This is the correct principle.
The matter that is the fruit of superior meditative concentration shall be briefly analyzed by way of seven categories.
First, regarding the arising [of these fruits] among ordinary beings and noble ones: as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*,
the "fruition of mastery" (*abhijñā-phala*) in the form realm can pertain to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
As stated in the thirty-third passage:
if a bodhisattva practicing vipaśyanā in the formless realm takes as their object the three realms and the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, there is a fixed color [of the tears] that falls like rain,
and because of the fragrance of the palace,
it must necessarily be a śrāvaka who is capable of such transformation.
Because these are not [exclusively] prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva],
they are accessible to both ordinary beings and sages, and all are capable of giving rise to them.
Whether they are functional or non-functional constitutes their distinction.
As stated in the Thirty-three [Verses]: Regarding the second, the basis (*āśraya*), there are two gates.
The first is the basis of the transformative [consciousness].
Second, regarding the basis of the transformed [mind]:
among the transforming [minds], it is common to all four dhyānas,
as stated in the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Viṃśatikā).
The supernormal power of meditative concentration (samādhi-bala-abhijñā) extends to the formless realms.
While it is reasonable that this applies to the six stages of the form realm and the four stages of the formless realm,
the seven other preparatory means (prayoga) are narrow and inferior in their operation.
Because there is no superior power capable of either delighting in or revulsion toward the higher or lower realms, one cannot transform them;
or because at the initial stage of the preparatory means, the signs have not yet arisen.
According to another interpretation, it is because the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception are subtle and obscure that one cannot do so.
Since the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) also lack universal pervasion, they likewise cannot [transform]. Above these,
depending on whether one relies on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
that which is transformed as the support— namely, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the uncontaminated— is definitely attained in all cases.
Because it conforms to that which undergoes transformation,
within the desire realm,
just as when the body is in a lower realm, the mind induces the matter resulting from meditative concentration.
Those [forms] belonging to the upper realms that resemble the category of form, as well as those that are untainted (anāsrava),
may not necessarily be perceived by the five consciousnesses of the desire realm;
these are termed "invisible and non-obstructive" (anidarśana-apratigha).
It may be so for the eighth object of the lower realm,
such as the eye and ear supernormal powers and their associated sensory bases;
there are many such instances.
If one who has attained the four dhyānas manifests a minor transformation of the desire realm,
capable of producing coarse matter resembling that of the desire realm,
it is for the sake of allowing the sentient beings of the desire realm to make use of it.
Thus, the objects of the five consciousnesses and the eighth [consciousness] are all bound to the desire realm,
because they arise as material fruits through the power of volitional inclination.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction.
The thirty-third [verse] states:

"The noble supernormal powers and transformations can cause enjoyments to be accomplished and bring about what is to be done. [This refers to] the three [types of existence], both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The transformations produced by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava) and cannot be used for practical purposes;
they can only be seen by others,
as stated in the *Triṃśikā*.
The transformations of the Noble Ones may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Among these, the fifth, eighth, and visual consciousnesses are exclusively contaminated.
Because their characteristics and conditions are identical,
they are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature; however,
when situated in the fruit, they are exclusively untainted wholesome (anāsrava-kuśala).
The same applies to both self and others.

The sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) transforms both self and others; it is common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and common to both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because they differ in their application to benefit and sport;
however, in the formless realm and in the intermediate state,
these are exclusively of a wholesome nature and do not include the fruit of retribution.
It is exclusively the object of meditative concentration;
for neutral concentration is incapable [of producing it].
Thus, the fruits of the four dhyānas include the neutral as well.
This exists prior to the seventh bhūmi for those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), but not for those from the eighth bhūmi onwards.

Fourth, regarding the presence or absence of objects and the non-transformation of the faculties, it is as explained in the *Abhidharma-kośa-vyākhyā* and other texts. Fifth, its nature is derived from the five great elements (*mahābhūta*).
As stated in the *Abhidharma-śāstra-ṭīkā*: "The six meditative absorptions (dhyāna) have both general and specific [classifications].
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā*: "Regarding that which is subsumed under the [eighteen] elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana):
it is the form (rūpa) transformed by the eighth consciousness, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), within the causal state."
The five consciousnesses cannot be definitively assigned to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
because [the relationship] is between the object and the sense faculty,
as well as between the effect and its cause.
Because all are definitively so;
the faculties that take them as objects are all the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*),
the element of mind (*manodhātu*), and the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The fruit is attributed to its cause because it is definitively subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*);
it is not subsumed among the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as a shadow follows from its substance.
Fifth, because they are not seen,
they may also be named after their objective bases (*dravya*),
such as visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
However, because there are instances where transformation occurs without depending on a material substrate,
the reflection is not subsumed under the category of following the substrate.
If this were to allow the five consciousnesses to experience [the object], [it would lead to logical fallacies].
This includes the five external bases as well as those subsumed under the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Those subsumed under the base of mental phenomena are as previously explained.
Regarding those subsumed under the five objects (*viṣaya*):
This is because the object is contrasted with the faculty;
it is explained by departing from the cause and following the result.
Thus, if the external objects of the five consciousnesses [are considered],...
Because the fruit follows from the cause,
it is called the "fruit of superior concentration" (*samādhi-phala*);
it is likewise subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The same applies to the mind (*manas*) and the eight [consciousnesses] that accompany it in their objective spheres.
Regarding the actual matter (*rūpa*) transformed by the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the seventh, and the eighth within the state of Buddhahood:
Because they arise from the five consciousnesses, they are all termed the "five objects" (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Otherwise, how could the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of the Buddha-fruit be called untainted (*anāsrava*)?
This is because it is extensively established in the *Buddhabhūmi* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Just as the five objects transformed by the seventh and eighth consciousnesses within the distracted mind are all five objects because they are [perceived as] the five objects,
so too are the provisional forms transformed by the seventh and eighth consciousnesses within the resultant consciousness of a Buddha.
Just as the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth can be included solely within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
if the five consciousnesses and their objects were likewise subsumed under the five external spheres,
why is it now stated that only the fruits of superior meditative concentration are mentioned specifically within the sphere of mental objects?
Because it exists as the fundamental matter within its cause,
the five [sensory consciousnesses] for the most part do not take it as their object;
being subtle by nature, it is called "invisible and non-obstructive" (*anidarśana-apratigha*).
If it is asserted that the five views are produced by supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth,
this refers to the matter (*rūpa*) in the "Section on the Dharmas that are Fruits of Superior Concentration" in the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
As for the accomplishment of the basis,
it is also seen by others;
that is to say, it is not invisible and non-obstructive.
It is not like "non-visible and non-obstructive" material forms,
which are named from their fundamental nature;
it does not mean that they do not exist in reality.
In the *Triṃśikā*, it is stated that because the meditative attainments (*samādhi*) of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) belonging to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can still be seen by others,
based on this very principle,
some say that the fruit of Buddhahood does not possess fifteen elements (*dhātu*).
If it were not so, the matter that is the fruit of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would not belong exclusively to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This is the interpretation of Dharmapāla and others.
Regarding the establishment of the truths within the causal stage,
because it speaks only of the existence of bases and elements,
it refers exclusively to the dharma-base as the fruit of supreme meditative concentration.
If it were not so, why would the Sūtra state that the eighteen elements (dhātus) include both the outflow-free (anāsrava) and the obtained eternal form (rūpa), and so forth?
Therefore, the former explanation is correct.
Among the [categories] such as transformation due to causes and conditions:
The commentary provides four explanations.
First, "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) has the meaning of spontaneity;
"discrimination" (vikalpa) has the meaning of forced conceptualization.
The Master Nanda [asserts that] the five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*),
are also capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*) and maintaining all seeds; their transformation is entirely functional,
immediately giving rise to various types of karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) like the sprouting of shoots.

The third volume below will provide a detailed explanation of why this is incorrect. As for the second [point], the "causes and conditions" refers to the actual causes and conditions of all phenomena;
the "discriminative" refers to the remaining seven consciousnesses.
Since it is not a real seed,
only that which is transformed by the eighth consciousness is taken as the transformation of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). What,
then, is the meaning of "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) here?
If one were to discuss its maturation (vipāka), it should properly be included among the five categories. Why is this not so?
If that which is transformed by the five consciousnesses is not a real dharma, [how could it be so?]
What is meant by "attaining the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
If one says that what is attained is the specific characteristic of the locus (*deśasvalakṣaṇa*) rather than the specific characteristic of the entity (*vastusvalakṣaṇa*),
then [characteristics] such as blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as the determined four great elements (*mahābhūta*), would not be attained by the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
It is most remarkably miraculous;
when the body is burned by fire, one should not perceive pain and so forth.
Furthermore, the fundamental consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) is established as being truly distinct from the five sensory consciousnesses.
It should therefore be subsumed under the five sense objects and the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), rather than being subsumed under the five [specific] objective domains.
If one grants that the five consciousnesses apprehend specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
then the general [characteristic] is included within the five sense objects by virtue of its dependence upon the particular ones.
Since it is not admitted that [the mind] takes its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as an object,
how can the provisional [nature] follow the real by being subsumed under the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*),
as in the case of the form resulting from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*)?
This is fundamentally a transformation of the mind alone;
even if the five consciousnesses are involved,
they are subsumed under the primary mind.
It is called the fruit of superior concentration (*viśeṣa-samādhi*).
It is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This refers to the derivative rather than the fundamental.
When objects are contrasted with the sense faculties,
they may be subsumed under the five sensory domains; however,
the five fundamental colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth, cannot be [so] obtained.
Since it is perceived solely by the mind, it should be subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
For what reason, then, is it subsumed under the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) based on the conventional rather than the ultimate? Regarding this, the third explanation states:
Regarding the causes and conditions: these are the resultant consciousnesses.
"Causes" refers to the seeds of names and phrases;
"conditions" refers to the conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
If it is argued that these transformations must necessarily have a function,
then the same should apply to the primary consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), and so forth as examples.
If it is argued that they are not [functions] because they lack autonomy, [then the same applies here].
Since the five consciousnesses are not at all times the fruit of karma,
the same applies to the concomitant manas;
how could their transformation necessarily have utility?
Furthermore, the "solitary" mind is the mind of karmic fruition;
because its causes and conditions undergo transformation, it must also possess functional efficacy.
For this reason, it is known that the fourth [type of] mind is wholesome.
Regarding "causes and conditions," the essence of dharmas truly arises from genuine seeds.
That which arises from genuine seeds possesses functional efficacy through its transformations.
The remainder are called "conceptualized.
Objective spheres do not follow the mind;
solitary images arise solely from the seeing-part.
The "concrete" (dai-zhi) [cognition] penetrates both the mental aspect and the objective basis;

the "nature-seed" (xing-zhong) and other [types of cognition] correspond accordingly. The nature-aspect and the objective basis in their entirety, as well as one part of the concrete [cognition], are transformations due to causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma).
The "solitary image" (*ekacchāyā*) and a portion of the "image with substance" (*sadravya*) are transformations through conceptualization (*vikalpa*). However,
the object of the "image with substance" may pertain to both the category of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the category of conceptualization.

Because it is subsumed under the two gates of seeds and seeing: if the mind as the object of perception lacks the function of cognition, how can the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) have a function when it takes the self-verifying division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) as its object?
Answer: This is because the meaning of "self-substance" (svabhāva-artha) pertains to the division itself and is not the objective image-division (nimitta-bhāga).
Regarding the phrase "transforming the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) into something equivalent would render it devoid of practical utility," the term "etc.
includes non-associated factors (*viprayuktadharma*).
The unconditioned lacks substantial reality.
What is equal and non-associated is useless;

these are combined into a single text, yet it is not that they are useless for being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). There are those who understand True Suchness (*tathatā*) but have not yet realized it.
If it were merely non-existent, it would be useless;

since both [the conditioned and the unconditioned] do not serve as objects of cognition, they are combined into a single textual expression and thus said to lack practical utility. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although True Suchness lacks a real, functional activity...
What is now called "function" refers to efficacy;
that is, the power of True Suchness (tathatā) to be free from bondage.
What is now called the "transformation of the fundamental consciousness into True Suchness" does not mean it becomes identical to its original essence.
The absence of the power of actual dissociation is what is meant by "uselessness";
it does not mean that there is no functional activity whatsoever.
This interpretation is correct.
Furthermore, even when images are presented, there is no actual utility within the mind;
therefore, it does not undergo transformation.
Thus, it is said that the eighth consciousness perceives three kinds of objects.
It is not said that the objects of the dharma-sphere are [exclusively] internal,
because they are the natural objects of focus for those who do not possess the power of meditative concentration; furthermore,
even if these objects of the dharma-sphere were transformed, they would not differ from the two categories of the internal body and the external vessel-world.
These two categories encompass everything.
